title: The Journey of the Word Sugar
description: Trace the word 'sugar' from ancient Sanskrit across trade routes through Persian, Arabic, and into European languages — revealing how a single commodity reshaped global vocabulary.
steps: [{"text":"The story begins in ancient India, where sugarcane was first cultivated in the Indus Valley and Ganges Plain. The Sanskrit word 'śarkarā' (शर्करा) originally meant 'ground or candied sugar', derived from a root meaning 'gravel' or 'grit'.","map_center":[25.0,82.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-500,"highlighted_entities":["san"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"As trade routes connected India to Persia, the word traveled westward. Old Persian adopted it as 'šakar', and Middle Persian refined it to 'shakar'. The Sassanid Empire became a key node in sugar production and linguistic transmission.","map_center":[32.0,53.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":300,"highlighted_entities":["pes"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"With the Islamic conquests and the flourishing of Arab trade networks, Arabic adopted the word as 'sukkar' (سكر). Arab merchants spread both the commodity and its name across the Mediterranean world during the Golden Age.","map_center":[30.0,45.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":800,"highlighted_entities":["arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Medieval Latin borrowed the Arabic term as 'succarum', which then branched into Old French 'sucre', Italian 'zucchero', and Spanish 'azúcar' (with the Arabic article 'al-' prefix). Each Romance language adapted the word to its phonological system.","map_center":[43.0,10.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1200,"highlighted_entities":["fra","ita","spa"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Middle English borrowed 'sucre' from Anglo-Norman French, eventually becoming modern English 'sugar'. Meanwhile, German adopted 'Zucker' through Italian trade contacts, and Russian borrowed 'сахар' (sakhar) through a separate eastern route.","map_center":[52.0,0.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1400,"highlighted_entities":["eng","deu","rus"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"By the colonial era, sugar plantations in the Caribbean and Americas drove the Atlantic slave trade, making 'sugar' one of history's most consequential loanwords — a single word connecting ancient India to the modern global economy.","map_center":[18.0,-66.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1700,"highlighted_entities":["eng","spa","fra","por"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}}]

title: How the Silk Road Changed Languages
description: Discover how the ancient Silk Road created a linguistic melting pot, facilitating the exchange of words, writing systems, and entire language families across Eurasia.
steps: [{"text":"The Silk Road begins at Chang'an (modern Xi'an), capital of the Han Dynasty. Chinese traders set out westward, carrying silk, paper, and words that would influence dozens of languages along the route.","map_center":[34.3,108.9],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-200,"highlighted_entities":["cmn"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"In the Tarim Basin oases, Tocharian languages (now extinct Indo-European languages spoken in western China) served as intermediaries. The word 'honey' (Tocharian B 'mit') shows deep Indo-European roots thriving far to the east of their expected range.","map_center":[40.5,80.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":200,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","archaeological_sites"]}},{"text":"Sogdian merchants from Samarkand became the Silk Road's great lingua franca speakers. Their Iranian language served as the trade language from China to Persia, leaving loanwords in Chinese, Turkic, and Mongolian languages.","map_center":[39.6,66.9],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":500,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"The spread of Buddhism along the Silk Road carried Sanskrit terminology into Chinese, Tibetan, Mongolian, and Southeast Asian languages. Words like 'Buddha', 'nirvana', and 'dharma' became global vocabulary through these trade networks.","map_center":[30.0,78.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":400,"highlighted_entities":["san"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","religions"]}},{"text":"Turkic languages spread along the Silk Road corridors as Turkic peoples migrated westward. Words for trade goods, animals, and governance passed between Turkic, Persian, Chinese, and Mongolian, creating a rich web of shared vocabulary.","map_center":[42.0,65.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":700,"highlighted_entities":["tur","uzb","kaz"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"By the Mongol Empire era, the Silk Road reached peak connectivity. Persian became the administrative language of much of the route, while Mongolian words entered Russian, Turkish, and even Korean — a testament to the road's linguistic legacy.","map_center":[47.0,100.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1250,"highlighted_entities":["pes","mon","rus"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes","civilizations"]}}]

title: The Indo-European Expansion
description: Follow the most successful language family in history as it spread from the Pontic Steppe to dominate Europe, Iran, and India over thousands of years.
steps: [{"text":"Around 4500 BCE on the Pontic-Caspian Steppe (modern Ukraine/southern Russia), speakers of Proto-Indo-European herded cattle, domesticated horses, and developed a language that would become the ancestor of nearly half the world's spoken languages.","map_center":[48.0,38.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-4500,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["archaeological_sites","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Yamnaya culture (c. 3300-2600 BCE) spread westward into Europe and eastward toward Central Asia. Their mastery of horse-drawn wheeled vehicles gave them unprecedented mobility. DNA evidence confirms massive population replacements across Europe.","map_center":[47.0,40.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":-3000,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["migrations","archaeological_sites","haplogroups"]}},{"text":"The Anatolian branch (including Hittite) was the first to diverge, establishing the Hittite Empire in modern Turkey by 1600 BCE. Hittite, written in cuneiform, is the oldest attested Indo-European language.","map_center":[39.5,34.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-1600,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Indo-Iranian speakers moved southeast, splitting into Iranian (ancestors of Persian, Kurdish, Pashto) and Indo-Aryan (ancestors of Sanskrit, Hindi, Bengali). The Rigveda, composed c. 1500-1200 BCE, preserves archaic Indo-European mythology and vocabulary.","map_center":[30.0,70.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":-1500,"highlighted_entities":["san","hin","fas"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"Celtic, Italic, Germanic, Slavic, and Baltic branches diversified across Europe. Latin spread through Roman conquest, later fracturing into the Romance languages — the linguistic heirs of an empire.","map_center":[45.0,12.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":-200,"highlighted_entities":["lat","fra","spa","por","ita"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Today, Indo-European languages are spoken by over 3.2 billion people as a first language. From Icelandic to Bengali, from Portuguese to Tajik — this single family's 6,500-year journey represents humanity's greatest linguistic expansion.","map_center":[40.0,30.0],"map_zoom":2,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["eng","hin","spa","por","ben","rus"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Columbian Exchange
description: Explore how the collision of Old and New World languages after 1492 created pidgins, creoles, and a torrent of loanwords that transformed vocabularies on every continent.
steps: [{"text":"Before Columbus, the Americas hosted extraordinary linguistic diversity — over 1,000 languages across hundreds of families. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan alone was a multilingual hub where Nahuatl served as the lingua franca of Mesoamerica.","map_center":[19.4,-99.1],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1490,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Spanish conquistadors in the Caribbean created the first sustained contact. Taíno words entered Spanish and then spread globally: 'hurricane' (hurakán), 'canoe' (canoa), 'hammock' (hamaca), 'barbecue' (barbacoa), and 'tobacco' (tabaco).","map_center":[19.0,-70.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":["spa"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"From Mexico, Nahuatl contributed 'chocolate' (chocolātl), 'tomato' (tomatl), 'avocado' (ahuacatl), and 'coyote' (coyōtl). These words traveled through Spanish into English, French, and dozens of other languages — food words following the food itself.","map_center":[19.4,-99.1],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1550,"highlighted_entities":["spa","eng","fra"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Quechua, the language of the Inca Empire, gave us 'condor' (kuntur), 'llama', 'quinoa' (kinwa), and 'jerky' (ch'arki). Portuguese carried these into global trade networks, while Quechua itself absorbed Spanish words and survived as a living language.","map_center":[-13.5,-72.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1540,"highlighted_entities":["que","spa","por"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"In the Caribbean and Americas, the collision of African, European, and Indigenous languages birthed creole languages — Haitian Creole, Papiamentu, Sranan Tongo — entirely new linguistic systems forged in the crucible of colonialism and slavery.","map_center":[18.5,-72.3],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1700,"highlighted_entities":["fra","spa","por"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"The Columbian Exchange made 'chocolate', 'potato', 'maize', and 'tobacco' universal vocabulary. No event in history has transferred more words between more languages in so short a time — a linguistic big bang still reverberating today.","map_center":[20.0,-30.0],"map_zoom":2,"time_point":1800,"highlighted_entities":["eng","spa","fra","por","deu","nld"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}}]

title: The Spread of Writing
description: Follow the invention and transmission of writing systems — from Sumerian cuneiform to the smartphone keyboard — and see how literacy reshaped language itself.
steps: [{"text":"Around 3400 BCE in Uruk (southern Mesopotamia), Sumerians developed cuneiform — pressing wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets. Initially for accounting, it evolved into the first full writing system, capable of recording literature, law, and language.","map_center":[31.3,45.6],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":-3400,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["archaeological_sites","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Independently, Egyptian hieroglyphs emerged around 3200 BCE. Meanwhile, cuneiform was adopted by Akkadians, Babylonians, Hittites, and Persians — each adapting the script to their own language, proving writing systems could be borrowed and modified.","map_center":[29.9,31.1],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-3200,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["civilizations","archaeological_sites"]}},{"text":"Around 1050 BCE, Phoenician traders developed the first alphabet — a revolutionary simplification reducing hundreds of cuneiform signs to ~22 letters. From ports like Byblos and Tyre, this alphabet spread across the Mediterranean world.","map_center":[34.1,35.6],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":-1050,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["trade_routes","civilizations"]}},{"text":"The Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet (~800 BCE), crucially adding vowel letters. This Greek alphabet became the ancestor of Latin (and thus all Western European scripts), Cyrillic (used across Slavic-speaking lands), and Coptic.","map_center":[37.9,23.7],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-800,"highlighted_entities":["grc"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"In South and Southeast Asia, the Brahmi script (c. 300 BCE) gave rise to Devanagari, Tamil, Thai, Tibetan, Khmer, and dozens more. A single Indian writing tradition birthed scripts used from Sri Lanka to Mongolia.","map_center":[25.0,80.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":-300,"highlighted_entities":["san","hin","tam"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Chinese characters, developed independently, spread to Japan (kanji), Korea (hanja), and Vietnam (chữ Hán). Today, writing has gone digital — but every text message traces its lineage to clay tablets pressed in ancient Sumer 5,400 years ago.","map_center":[35.0,110.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":100,"highlighted_entities":["cmn","jpn","kor","vie"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: Bantu Migration and Language Diversification
description: Follow one of history's great migrations as Bantu-speaking peoples expanded across sub-Saharan Africa over 3,000 years, carrying iron-working, agriculture, and a language family now spoken by 350 million people.
steps: [{"text":"Around 3000 BCE, Proto-Bantu speakers lived in the Cameroon-Nigeria borderlands. They were farmers who cultivated yams and oil palms. Their language would become the ancestor of over 500 languages spanning half a continent.","map_center":[6.0,10.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-3000,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The first wave moved south and east through the Congo rainforest (c. 2000-1000 BCE), adapting to new environments. As groups separated by dense forest, their languages began to diverge — the first splits in what would become a vast language family.","map_center":[0.0,20.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-1500,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["migrations","languages"]}},{"text":"Emerging from the forest into the Great Lakes region (c. 1000 BCE), Bantu speakers encountered pastoralist Nilotic and Cushitic peoples. Languages mixed and borrowed: cattle terminology from Nilotic languages entered Bantu vocabularies, while Bantu farming words influenced neighbors.","map_center":[-2.0,32.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-1000,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"Iron-working technology (possibly acquired from Nok culture contacts) accelerated the expansion. By 500 CE, Bantu speakers had reached southern Africa. Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, and Shona all descend from these migrants — sister languages separated by centuries of divergence.","map_center":[-15.0,28.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":500,"highlighted_entities":["zul","xho","sot","sna"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Swahili coast (c. 800 CE) shows Bantu languages meeting the Indian Ocean world. Swahili, a Bantu language, absorbed massive Arabic vocabulary through trade — words for 'book' (kitabu), 'time' (wakati), and 'number' (nambari) all have Arabic origins.","map_center":[-6.8,39.3],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":800,"highlighted_entities":["swh","arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Today, Bantu languages are spoken by ~350 million people across 24 countries. From Zulu click consonants (borrowed from Khoisan neighbors) to Swahili's Arabic loanwords, this family illustrates how migration and contact continuously reshape languages.","map_center":[-5.0,25.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["swh","zul","sna","lin","nya"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Norman Conquest and English
description: See how the Battle of Hastings in 1066 split English into two — the language of the conquered and the language of the court — and how their merger created the rich hybrid tongue we speak today.
steps: [{"text":"Before 1066, Old English was a fully Germanic language — closer to modern Dutch or German than to modern English. Words like 'house', 'bread', 'water', 'good', and 'friend' come from this Anglo-Saxon core that has survived a thousand years.","map_center":[52.0,-1.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1050,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"On October 14, 1066, William of Normandy defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings. The Norman French-speaking elite replaced the English aristocracy virtually overnight. French became the language of law, court, government, and prestige.","map_center":[50.9,0.5],"map_zoom":7,"time_point":1066,"highlighted_entities":["eng","fra"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","battles"]}},{"text":"For nearly 300 years, England was linguistically stratified: peasants spoke English, nobles spoke French, and the church used Latin. This created famous doublets: English 'cow' vs. French 'beef', 'sheep' vs. 'mutton', 'pig' vs. 'pork' — the animal in the field vs. the meat on the table.","map_center":[51.5,-0.1],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1200,"highlighted_entities":["eng","fra"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) and the Black Death (1348) paradoxically revived English. French became the enemy's language; labor shortages empowered English-speaking workers. By 1362, English was officially used in Parliament for the first time since the Conquest.","map_center":[51.5,-0.1],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1362,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Middle English emerged as a true hybrid: Germanic grammar and core vocabulary fused with thousands of French loanwords. Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (c. 1390) showcases this new language — unmistakably English, yet saturated with French-origin words for law, art, food, and fashion.","map_center":[51.3,1.1],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1390,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Modern English vocabulary is roughly 29% French-origin, 29% Latin, and 26% Germanic. The Norman Conquest gave English its extraordinary synonym richness: 'begin/commence', 'ask/demand', 'freedom/liberty' — Germanic and Romance twins expressing subtle shades of meaning.","map_center":[51.5,-0.1],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: Austronesian Voyagers
description: Follow the greatest maritime expansion in human history — Austronesian-speaking peoples who colonized half the planet's longitude, from Madagascar to Easter Island, guided by stars and language.
steps: [{"text":"Around 3000 BCE, Austronesian-speaking peoples from Taiwan began the most remarkable maritime expansion in human history. These Neolithic farmers and master sailors would eventually settle islands spanning more than half the Earth's circumference.","map_center":[23.5,121.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":-3000,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"By 2000 BCE, Austronesians had reached the Philippines and Indonesia, establishing the languages that would become Tagalog, Malay, Javanese, and hundreds more. Shared words for 'outrigger canoe', 'sail', and 'navigate' reveal their maritime focus.","map_center":[5.0,120.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":-2000,"highlighted_entities":["tgl","msa","jav"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Lapita culture carried Austronesian languages into Oceania (c. 1500 BCE), reaching Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa. These became the Polynesian homeland — 'Hawaiki' in their oral traditions — where the Polynesian branch of languages crystallized.","map_center":[-15.0,175.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":-1500,"highlighted_entities":["ton","smo"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations","archaeological_sites"]}},{"text":"In an astonishing western voyage, Austronesians crossed the entire Indian Ocean to settle Madagascar (c. 500 CE). Malagasy, the island's language, is not African but Austronesian — more closely related to languages in Borneo than to any language on mainland Africa.","map_center":[-18.9,47.5],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":500,"highlighted_entities":["mlg"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"Polynesians reached Hawai'i (c. 800 CE), Aotearoa/New Zealand (c. 1250 CE), and Rapa Nui/Easter Island (c. 1200 CE), completing a triangle spanning thousands of miles of open ocean. Hawaiian, Māori, and Rapanui remain mutually recognizable to trained linguists.","map_center":[-10.0,-160.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1200,"highlighted_entities":["haw","mri"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"Today, over 1,200 Austronesian languages are spoken by 400 million people — the second-largest language family by number of languages. From Madagascar to Easter Island, a single family's voyaging legacy spans 206 degrees of longitude.","map_center":[0.0,140.0],"map_zoom":2,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["msa","tgl","jav","mlg","mri","haw"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Arabic Golden Age
description: Explore how Arabic became the language of science, philosophy, and innovation during the Islamic Golden Age, preserving Greek knowledge and transmitting it — with Arabic vocabulary — to medieval Europe.
steps: [{"text":"After the rise of Islam in the 7th century, Arabic rapidly expanded from a regional language of the Arabian Peninsula to become the lingua franca of an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia. The Quran's language became a unifying force.","map_center":[24.5,39.6],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":650,"highlighted_entities":["arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"The Abbasid Caliphate's House of Wisdom in Baghdad (c. 800-1258 CE) became the world's greatest center of learning. Scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic — Aristotle, Ptolemy, Galen, and the Indian numeral system all passed through Arabic.","map_center":[33.3,44.4],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":830,"highlighted_entities":["arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Arabic scientific terminology spread globally. 'Algebra' (al-jabr), 'algorithm' (al-Khwarizmi), 'alchemy' (al-kīmiyā), 'alcohol' (al-kuḥl), 'zenith' (samt), 'nadir' (naẓīr) — these Arabic-origin words reveal who was doing cutting-edge science.","map_center":[33.3,44.4],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":900,"highlighted_entities":["arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"In Al-Andalus (Islamic Spain), Arabic coexisted with Romance languages for centuries. The result: Spanish absorbed ~4,000 Arabic loanwords — 'almohada' (pillow), 'aceite' (oil), 'aldea' (village). The 'al-' prefix marks Arabic's fingerprint on Spanish.","map_center":[37.4,-5.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1000,"highlighted_entities":["arb","spa"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"The Toledo School of Translators (12th-13th century) translated Arabic scientific texts into Latin, transmitting centuries of Arabic scholarship to medieval Europe. This was the funnel through which Greek philosophy — preserved and enriched by Arabic scholars — re-entered Western thought.","map_center":[39.9,-4.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1175,"highlighted_entities":["arb","spa","lat"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Arabic's legacy in global vocabulary is immense: English 'cotton', 'magazine', 'tariff', 'admiral', 'zero', and 'coffee' all trace to Arabic. The language of the Golden Age didn't just preserve ancient knowledge — it created new knowledge and the words to describe it.","map_center":[30.0,35.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1300,"highlighted_entities":["arb","eng","spa","fra","por"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}}]

title: The Spice Trade
description: Follow the spice routes that connected the Moluccas to Venice, spreading not just pepper and cinnamon but the words for them — a story of how commerce creates shared vocabulary across unrelated languages.
steps: [{"text":"The Spice Islands (Maluku, eastern Indonesia) were the world's only source of cloves, nutmeg, and mace. Malay traders created a maritime trade network spanning Southeast Asia, establishing Malay as the region's trade lingua franca long before European contact.","map_center":[-1.5,128.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":100,"highlighted_entities":["msa"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Indian Ocean monsoon winds connected Southeast Asia to India, Arabia, and East Africa. Tamil, Arabic, and Malay merchants met at entrepôts like Calicut and Malacca. The Malay word 'kampung' (village) entered English as 'compound'; Tamil 'kari' became 'curry'.","map_center":[10.0,76.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":800,"highlighted_entities":["tam","msa","arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Arabic merchants dominated the western Indian Ocean spice trade for centuries. Arabic 'qirfa' (cinnamon), 'qaranful' (clove), and 'za'faran' (saffron) influenced trade vocabulary across the Mediterranean. 'Saffron' entered English via Arabic from Persian.","map_center":[23.0,55.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1100,"highlighted_entities":["arb","pes"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Venice and Genoa monopolized Europe's spice access through Alexandria. Italian commercial vocabulary spread: 'traffic' (from Arabic tafriq via Italian traffico), 'risk' (Italian risco, possibly from Arabic rizq). The spice trade was literally building the language of commerce.","map_center":[45.4,12.3],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1300,"highlighted_entities":["ita","arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, breaking the Arab-Venetian spice monopoly. Portuguese traders established forts from Goa to Malacca to the Moluccas, and Portuguese pidgin became the first global trade language — ancestor of several Asian creoles.","map_center":[10.0,76.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":["por","msa"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"The Dutch VOC (founded 1602) seized the spice trade, making Malay an administrative language and borrowing terms like 'bamboo' (bambu), 'gong', and 'orangutan' (orang utan, 'forest person'). The quest for spices drove European colonialism and permanently reshaped world languages.","map_center":[0.0,110.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1650,"highlighted_entities":["nld","msa","eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}}]

title: The Journey of Coffee
description: Follow the word 'coffee' from Ethiopian highlands through Arabic 'qahwa' to Turkish 'kahve' and into every European language — a caffeinated tour of global linguistic borrowing.
steps: [{"text":"The story of coffee begins in the Ethiopian highlands, where the Kaffa region gave the beverage its name. According to legend, a goatherd named Kaldi noticed his goats dancing after eating certain berries. The Oromo people of Ethiopia were among the first to cultivate coffee.","map_center":[7.5,36.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":900,"highlighted_entities":["orm"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Sufi mystics in Yemen adopted coffee as an aid to nighttime devotion in the 15th century. Arabic transformed the word into 'qahwa' (قهوة), originally a term for wine. The port of Mocha (Al-Makha) became synonymous with coffee trade, and its name survives in 'mocha' worldwide.","map_center":[13.3,43.3],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1450,"highlighted_entities":["arb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"The Ottoman Empire embraced coffee culture, and Turkish 'kahve' became the direct source for most European words. Istanbul's coffeehouses (kahvehane) were centers of intellectual life. The Turkish pronunciation shaped how Europe would say this word for centuries.","map_center":[41.0,29.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1550,"highlighted_entities":["tur"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Italian traders in Venice were among the first Europeans to import coffee (c. 1600). Italian 'caffè' passed to French 'café', Spanish 'café', and Portuguese 'café'. The word traveled the same routes as the beans — through Mediterranean trade networks.","map_center":[45.4,12.3],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1620,"highlighted_entities":["ita","fra","spa","por"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"English borrowed 'coffee' from Dutch 'koffie' (itself from Turkish) in the 1650s. London coffeehouses became 'penny universities' where ideas flowed freely. German 'Kaffee', Swedish 'kaffe', and Russian 'кофе' (kofe) all trace back through the same Turkish-Arabic chain.","map_center":[51.5,-0.1],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1660,"highlighted_entities":["eng","nld","deu","rus"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Colonial plantations spread coffee — and its name — to Java (giving English 'java'), Brazil, and Colombia. Today the word exists in virtually every language on Earth: Japanese 'コーヒー' (kōhī), Hindi 'कॉफ़ी' (kofī), Swahili 'kahawa' — all echoes of that Ethiopian origin.","map_center":[0.0,30.0],"map_zoom":2,"time_point":1800,"highlighted_entities":["jpn","hin","swh","por","eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}}]

title: The Viking Linguistic Trail
description: Follow the Norse raiders and traders who left an indelible mark on English, French, Russian, and languages across the North Atlantic — from 'berserk' to 'Bluetooth'.
steps: [{"text":"In the late 8th century, Old Norse-speaking Vikings erupted from Scandinavia. Their language, a North Germanic tongue, would leave traces across half of Europe. The word 'Viking' itself may come from Old Norse 'vík' (inlet) — these were people of the fjords.","map_center":[60.0,11.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":780,"highlighted_entities":["nor","swe","dan"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Danelaw era (865-954 CE) saw Norse settlers occupying eastern England. Old Norse and Old English were similar enough for mutual intelligibility, and they merged freely. Everyday English words like 'sky', 'egg', 'take', 'they', 'their', and 'them' are Norse gifts.","map_center":[54.0,-1.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":900,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"In 911 CE, Viking leader Rollo was granted Normandy ('Northman-land') by the French king. The Norse settlers adopted French but left traces: Norman French vocabulary that later entered English through the 1066 conquest carried buried Norse elements alongside its French ones.","map_center":[49.4,1.1],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":911,"highlighted_entities":["fra"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"Varangian Vikings traveled east along Russian rivers to Constantinople. Old Norse 'Rus' may have given Russia its name. Norse traders established Kyiv and Novgorod, and Old Norse loanwords entered Slavic languages — but the Vikings were ultimately absorbed into Slavic culture.","map_center":[50.4,30.5],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":880,"highlighted_entities":["rus"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes","migrations"]}},{"text":"Norse settlers colonized Iceland (874 CE), Greenland (985 CE), and briefly North America (c. 1000 CE). Icelandic has changed so little that modern Icelanders can read the medieval sagas — a 1,000-year-old language preserved in volcanic isolation.","map_center":[64.1,-21.9],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1000,"highlighted_entities":["isl"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Viking linguistic legacy is enormous: English has over 1,000 Norse-origin words including 'window' (vindauga, 'wind-eye'), 'husband' (húsbóndi, 'house-dweller'), and 'berserk' (berserker, 'bear-shirt'). Place names ending in -by, -thorpe, and -thwaite map the Danelaw to this day.","map_center":[55.0,0.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1100,"highlighted_entities":["eng","nor","isl","dan","swe"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Persian Literary Empire
description: Discover how Persian became the language of poetry, diplomacy, and culture from Istanbul to Delhi — an empire of literature that transcended political boundaries for a thousand years.
steps: [{"text":"After the Arab conquest of Persia (651 CE), the Persian language nearly vanished under Arabic dominance. But Persian survived by reinventing itself: adopting the Arabic script, absorbing Arabic vocabulary, and emerging as New Persian — a language transformed but unbroken.","map_center":[32.7,51.7],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":700,"highlighted_entities":["fas"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (c. 1010 CE), the Persian 'Book of Kings', deliberately used minimal Arabic vocabulary to prove Persian's literary power. This 50,000-couplet epic became the cultural cornerstone of the Persian-speaking world, from Tajikistan to Kurdistan.","map_center":[35.3,59.6],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1010,"highlighted_entities":["fas"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Under Seljuk and Timurid patronage, Persian became Central Asia's prestige language. Rumi (d. 1273), writing in Persian in Anatolia, produced poetry still read worldwide. Persian 'divan' (poetry collection), 'ghazal', and 'rubai' became literary terms across multiple languages.","map_center":[37.9,32.5],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1250,"highlighted_entities":["fas","tur"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"The Mughal Empire (1526-1857) made Persian the administrative and literary language of the Indian subcontinent. Urdu emerged as a hybrid of Hindi grammar and massive Persian-Arabic vocabulary. Words like 'pajama' (pāy-jāmeh), 'bazaar' (bāzār), and 'khaki' (khākī) entered English through this Persian-Indian connection.","map_center":[28.6,77.2],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1600,"highlighted_entities":["fas","urd","hin"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Ottoman Turkish absorbed so much Persian and Arabic that Ottoman court language was nearly incomprehensible to common Turks. Persian words for abstract concepts, emotions, and art saturated Turkish, Azerbaijani, and Uzbek — the linguistic reach of Persian poetry transcended ethnic boundaries.","map_center":[41.0,29.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":["tur","fas","azb","uzb"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Today, Persian's literary legacy lives in three national varieties — Farsi (Iran), Dari (Afghanistan), and Tajik (Tajikistan) — plus thousands of loanwords in Turkish, Urdu, Hindi, Bengali, and even English. 'Paradise' (pardis), 'chess' (shah), and 'checkmate' (shah mat) are all Persian gifts to the world.","map_center":[35.0,55.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["fas","tgk","urd","tur","eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Dravidian Legacy
description: Explore the ancient Dravidian language family of South India — older than Indo-European presence in the subcontinent, with possible links to the Indus Valley Civilization and a living legacy of 250 million speakers.
steps: [{"text":"The Dravidian language family, with over 80 languages and 250 million speakers, predates the arrival of Indo-European languages in South Asia. Proto-Dravidian may have been spoken as early as 4500 BCE, making it one of the world's oldest traceable language families.","map_center":[13.0,77.5],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-4500,"highlighted_entities":["tam","tel","kan","mal"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"The Indus Valley Civilization (3300-1300 BCE) remains undeciphered, but many scholars believe its language was Dravidian. The geographic overlap between Indus sites and later Dravidian populations, plus structural analysis of the script, supports this tantalizing hypothesis.","map_center":[27.3,68.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-2500,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["archaeological_sites","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Tamil, the oldest attested Dravidian language, has a literary tradition spanning over 2,000 years. Sangam literature (300 BCE - 300 CE) preserves a sophisticated poetic tradition. Tamil is one of the world's few classical languages with an unbroken literary continuity.","map_center":[10.8,78.7],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":-200,"highlighted_entities":["tam"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Dravidian languages influenced Indo-Aryan languages profoundly. Sanskrit and Hindi acquired retroflexed consonants (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ), a distinctly Dravidian feature absent from other Indo-European branches. This phonological exchange reveals millennia of deep bilingual contact.","map_center":[20.0,78.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":500,"highlighted_entities":["tam","hin","san"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Brahui, a Dravidian language spoken in Pakistan and Afghanistan, sits 1,500 km from its nearest relatives — linguistic evidence of the family's once-wider range. Meanwhile, Telugu became the most-spoken Dravidian language, and Kannada and Malayalam developed rich literary traditions.","map_center":[28.0,66.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1000,"highlighted_entities":["tel","kan","mal"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Today, four Dravidian languages (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) have official status in Indian states. Dravidian loanwords in English include 'curry' (Tamil kaṟi), 'mango' (Tamil māṅgāy via Portuguese), and 'catamaran' (Tamil kaṭṭumaram, 'tied logs'). A family older than recorded history thrives in the modern world.","map_center":[13.0,78.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["tam","tel","kan","mal"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: Greek: The Language of Science
description: Trace how ancient Greek became the foundation of scientific, medical, and philosophical vocabulary worldwide — a dead language whose words are coined daily in laboratories and hospitals.
steps: [{"text":"Classical Athens (5th century BCE) developed the vocabulary of Western thought. Plato, Aristotle, and their contemporaries created terms that still define how we think: 'philosophy' (love of wisdom), 'democracy' (people-power), 'atom' (uncuttable), 'cosmos' (ordered universe).","map_center":[37.97,23.72],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":-450,"highlighted_entities":["grc"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Alexander's conquests (334-323 BCE) spread Koine Greek from Egypt to Afghanistan. Greek became the lingua franca of scholarship across the Hellenistic world. The Library of Alexandria, operating in Greek, became humanity's first universal knowledge repository.","map_center":[31.2,29.9],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":-300,"highlighted_entities":["grc"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Hippocrates and Galen established Greek as the language of medicine. 'Diagnosis', 'prognosis', 'symptom', 'therapy', 'anatomy', 'chronic', 'pandemic' — virtually every medical term is Greek. When Arabic scholars translated these texts, they preserved and extended the Greek medical lexicon.","map_center":[36.9,27.3],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-400,"highlighted_entities":["grc"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"The Roman Empire adopted Greek learning wholesale. Latin absorbed thousands of Greek terms, then transmitted them to all Romance languages. 'School' (Greek scholē via Latin schola), 'church' (Greek kyriakon), and 'angel' (Greek angelos) show Greek's path through Latin into modern European languages.","map_center":[41.9,12.5],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":100,"highlighted_entities":["grc","lat"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"The Renaissance and Scientific Revolution revived Greek as the source for new terminology. Scientists consistently turned to Greek roots: 'telescope' (far-seeing), 'microscope' (small-seeing), 'oxygen' (acid-forming), 'biology' (life-study), 'photograph' (light-writing).","map_center":[45.0,10.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1600,"highlighted_entities":["ell","eng","fra","deu"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Today, Greek roots generate new words at an accelerating pace: 'cybernetics', 'genomics', 'nanotechnology', 'cryptocurrency'. International scientific nomenclature is built on Greek. A language last spoken natively in the ancient world remains the most productive source of new vocabulary in modern science.","map_center":[37.97,23.72],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["ell","eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Birth of Creole Languages
description: Witness how colonial contact, slavery, and trade forged entirely new languages — Creoles that are not broken versions of their parents but innovative linguistic systems in their own right.
steps: [{"text":"When speakers of mutually unintelligible languages must communicate, they create pidgins — simplified trade languages with minimal grammar. But when children grow up speaking a pidgin as their first language, something remarkable happens: it becomes a creole, a fully complex natural language.","map_center":[15.0,-40.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Haitian Creole, born on sugar plantations from French and West African languages, is today spoken by 12 million people. Its grammar draws from Fon and Ewe (West African languages), while most vocabulary comes from French — but it is neither French nor African. It is something entirely new.","map_center":[18.9,-72.3],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1700,"highlighted_entities":["fra"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Portuguese-based creoles spread across the tropics through the slave trade and maritime commerce. Papiamentu (Aruba, Curaçao), Cape Verdean Creole, Kristang (Malacca), and Macanese reveal Portuguese as the first European language to seed creoles worldwide.","map_center":[12.2,-68.9],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1600,"highlighted_entities":["por"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"Tok Pisin in Papua New Guinea evolved from an English-based Pacific pidgin into a national language spoken by 4 million people. Its name comes from English 'talk pidgin'. Words like 'gras bilong het' (hair, literally 'grass belong head') show creative restructuring of English vocabulary.","map_center":[-6.0,147.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1850,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Gullah Geechee, spoken in the Sea Islands of South Carolina and Georgia, preserves more African linguistic features than any other English-based creole in the US. Its survival provides a direct linguistic link to the West African languages of enslaved peoples.","map_center":[32.0,-80.9],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1750,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Creole languages challenge the myth that they are 'broken' versions of European languages. Linguists now recognize them as fully complex systems that reveal universal principles of language creation. There are over 100 creole languages worldwide — living proof of human linguistic creativity under extreme conditions.","map_center":[10.0,-30.0],"map_zoom":2,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["fra","eng","por","spa","nld"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Uralic Journey
description: Discover the surprising family that connects Finnish, Hungarian, and languages spoken across the Arctic — a 7,000-year story of migration from the Ural Mountains to the heart of Europe.
steps: [{"text":"Around 5000 BCE, Proto-Uralic speakers lived near the Ural Mountains, between modern Russia and western Siberia. Their language would eventually split into a family spanning from Norway's Arctic coast to the Hungarian plains — one of linguistics' most surprising connections.","map_center":[58.0,58.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-5000,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Finno-Ugric branch migrated westward, reaching the Baltic region by 3000 BCE. Proto-Finnic peoples encountered Baltic and Germanic speakers, borrowing extensively. Finnish 'kuningas' (king) comes from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz — an ancient loan revealing centuries of contact.","map_center":[60.0,25.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-3000,"highlighted_entities":["fin","est"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Sámi peoples spread across northern Scandinavia, developing reindeer herding cultures. Their languages feature extraordinary precision for snow and ice — Sámi languages distinguish dozens of snow types — reflecting deep environmental adaptation encoded in vocabulary.","map_center":[69.0,25.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-1000,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"The Magyar migration (c. 896 CE) brought Hungarian — a Uralic language — into the heart of Europe. Surrounded by Slavic, Germanic, and Romance languages, Hungarian stubbornly preserved its Uralic core while borrowing vocabulary from every neighbor. The result is one of Europe's most distinctive languages.","map_center":[47.5,19.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":896,"highlighted_entities":["hun"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","migrations"]}},{"text":"Finnish and Hungarian share deep cognates invisible to casual observers: Finnish 'vesi' / Hungarian 'víz' (water), Finnish 'kala' / Hungarian 'hal' (fish), Finnish 'käsi' / Hungarian 'kéz' (hand). Six thousand years of separation have disguised the family resemblance.","map_center":[55.0,35.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":["fin","hun","est"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Today, the Uralic family includes ~38 languages spoken by 25 million people. Finnish and Estonian are thriving national languages, while many smaller Uralic languages in Russia face extinction. This family reminds us that Europe's linguistic map extends far beyond the Indo-European mainstream.","map_center":[55.0,40.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["fin","est","hun"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: Languages of the Roof of the World
description: Ascend into the Himalayan highlands where Sino-Tibetan languages diversified in extreme isolation, creating one of the world's most linguistically dense regions across the highest mountains on Earth.
steps: [{"text":"The Sino-Tibetan language family, second only to Indo-European in speaker count, originated somewhere along the Yellow River-Yangtze corridor around 7000 BCE. This family would eventually split into Chinese on one side and Tibeto-Burman on the other, separated by the world's highest mountains.","map_center":[33.0,100.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-7000,"highlighted_entities":["cmn","bod"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Tibetan developed its own script (c. 650 CE), adapted from Indian Brahmi through the efforts of Thonmi Sambhota. Classical Tibetan became the language of Buddhist scholarship, translating the entire Buddhist canon from Sanskrit and preserving texts lost in their original language.","map_center":[29.6,91.1],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":650,"highlighted_entities":["bod"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","religions"]}},{"text":"The Himalayan valleys created extraordinary linguistic diversity through isolation. Nepal alone hosts over 120 languages, many Tibeto-Burman, spoken in valleys just kilometers apart. Steep terrain meant that neighboring villages sometimes spoke mutually unintelligible languages.","map_center":[28.0,84.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1000,"highlighted_entities":["nep"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Burmese, another major Tibeto-Burman language, developed its distinctive script from Mon (itself derived from Indian scripts). The Bagan Empire (1044-1287) made Burmese a literary language, and it preserves tone patterns that help linguists reconstruct Proto-Sino-Tibetan.","map_center":[21.2,95.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1100,"highlighted_entities":["mya"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Northeast India is a linguistic treasure trove where Sino-Tibetan, Indo-European, Austroasiatic, and Tai-Kadai families converge. Languages like Mizo, Manipuri, and Nagamese represent centuries of contact and diversification in one of the world's most complex linguistic zones.","map_center":[25.5,93.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Today, Sino-Tibetan languages are spoken by over 1.5 billion people, with Mandarin Chinese accounting for most speakers. But the family's true diversity lies in the highlands: hundreds of small Tibeto-Burman languages, many unwritten and endangered, preserving linguistic structures found nowhere else on Earth.","map_center":[30.0,95.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["cmn","bod","mya","nep"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: The Printing Press and Language Standardization
description: See how Gutenberg's invention froze dialects into national languages, empowered vernaculars over Latin, and created the linguistic borders of modern Europe.
steps: [{"text":"Before printing, every manuscript was unique. Scribes copied texts by hand, introducing variations with each copy. Dialects shifted fluidly across landscapes with no 'correct' form. In 1450, Johannes Gutenberg's movable type press in Mainz would change language itself forever.","map_center":[50.0,8.3],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1450,"highlighted_entities":["deu"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Martin Luther's German Bible (1534) was a linguistic revolution. He chose a central German dialect (East Central German) that could be widely understood, and printing spread it uniformly. Luther essentially created modern standard German — a language born not from a court but from a printing press.","map_center":[51.0,11.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1534,"highlighted_entities":["deu"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","religions"]}},{"text":"In England, William Caxton's printing press (1476) standardized English spelling and vocabulary. He chose the London dialect as his standard, marginalizing northern and western forms. English spelling was frozen in the 15th century — which is why 'knight' still has a silent K and GH.","map_center":[51.5,-0.1],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1476,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"France took standardization further: the Académie Française (1635) was founded to regulate the French language. Parisian French became the national standard, and regional languages like Occitan, Breton, and Basque were actively suppressed. Printing made linguistic centralization possible and enforceable.","map_center":[48.9,2.3],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1635,"highlighted_entities":["fra"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Printing empowered vernacular languages at Latin's expense. Before 1500, ~77% of printed books were in Latin. By 1600, vernacular printing dominated. Scientific works shifted from Latin to national languages — Newton's Principia (1687) was among the last major works in Latin.","map_center":[48.0,10.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1600,"highlighted_entities":["deu","fra","eng","ita","spa"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"The printing press created the modern concept of 'a language' as a bounded, standardized system. Before printing, French and Italian formed a dialect continuum. After standardization, they became distinct national languages with borders, grammars, and dictionaries. We still live in the linguistic world the printing press made.","map_center":[48.0,8.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1750,"highlighted_entities":["fra","deu","eng","ita","spa","por","nld"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: Chinese Characters Across East Asia
description: Follow the spread of Chinese writing from the Oracle Bones of Shang dynasty to Japan, Korea, and Vietnam — and see how each culture adapted, transformed, and sometimes replaced this shared script.
steps: [{"text":"The earliest Chinese characters appear on oracle bones (c. 1200 BCE) from the Shang dynasty, used for divination. These pictographic and ideographic symbols evolved into a writing system that would become the longest continuously used script in human history.","map_center":[34.8,114.3],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":-1200,"highlighted_entities":["cmn"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","archaeological_sites"]}},{"text":"The Qin dynasty's unification (221 BCE) standardized Chinese characters across the empire. Emperor Qin Shi Huang mandated a single script (Small Seal), destroying regional variants. This political act ensured that speakers of mutually unintelligible Chinese dialects could communicate through shared writing.","map_center":[34.3,108.9],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":-221,"highlighted_entities":["cmn"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","civilizations"]}},{"text":"Japan adopted Chinese characters (kanji) beginning around the 5th century CE, using them to write a completely unrelated language. The mismatch led to creative solutions: each kanji acquired both Chinese-derived (on'yomi) and native Japanese (kun'yomi) readings — a dual system still used today.","map_center":[34.7,135.5],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":500,"highlighted_entities":["jpn"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Japan developed kana syllabaries (hiragana and katakana) in the 9th century by simplifying Chinese characters. This innovation allowed Japanese to be written with a mix of logographic kanji and phonetic kana — one of the world's most complex writing systems, born from the tension between Chinese script and Japanese speech.","map_center":[35.0,135.8],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":850,"highlighted_entities":["jpn"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Korea used Chinese characters (hanja) for centuries until King Sejong created Hangul in 1443 — a scientifically designed alphabet encoding Korean phonology. Sejong explicitly sought to free Korea from dependence on Chinese script, calling it unsuitable for the Korean language. Hangul is widely considered one of the most brilliant writing systems ever invented.","map_center":[37.6,127.0],"map_zoom":6,"time_point":1443,"highlighted_entities":["kor"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"Vietnam used Chinese characters (chữ Hán) and a derivative script (chữ Nôm) until French colonizers introduced the Latin-based chữ Quốc ngữ in the 17th-20th centuries. Today, of the four major East Asian cultures that adopted Chinese characters, each found a different solution: Japan kept them, Korea replaced them, Vietnam romanized, and China simplified them.","map_center":[21.0,105.8],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1900,"highlighted_entities":["vie","jpn","kor","cmn"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]

title: Languages of the Atlantic Slave Trade
description: Trace how the forced displacement of millions of Africans created a linguistic upheaval — destroying some languages, transforming others, and giving birth to entirely new ones across the Americas.
steps: [{"text":"Before the Atlantic slave trade, West and Central Africa hosted extraordinary linguistic diversity. The Niger-Congo family alone contained over 1,500 languages. Enslaved peoples were deliberately mixed across language groups to prevent communication and rebellion — a linguistic weapon of control.","map_center":[8.0,2.0],"map_zoom":4,"time_point":1500,"highlighted_entities":[],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"On slave ships, speakers of Wolof, Yoruba, Igbo, Fon, Akan, and Kikongo were thrown together. Survival demanded rapid communication. Shipboard pidgins emerged — simplified trade languages drawing from Portuguese, English, and West African grammatical structures.","map_center":[10.0,-25.0],"map_zoom":3,"time_point":1600,"highlighted_entities":["por","eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","trade_routes"]}},{"text":"In Brazil, enslaved Africans brought Yoruba and Bantu languages that deeply influenced Brazilian Portuguese. Words like 'samba', 'axé', 'dendê', 'quiabo' (okra), and 'moleque' (kid) are African-origin. Candomblé religious ceremonies preserve Yoruba language in ritual contexts to this day.","map_center":[-12.9,-38.5],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1700,"highlighted_entities":["por"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages","religions"]}},{"text":"In the Caribbean, plantation creoles crystallized. Jamaican Patois, Trinidadian Creole, and Barbadian Bajan draw English vocabulary but structure sentences using West African grammatical patterns: serial verb constructions, topic-comment structure, and tense-mood-aspect markers from Akan, Igbo, and Yoruba.","map_center":[18.1,-77.3],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1750,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"In the US South, African linguistic influence shaped the English spoken by all Southerners, Black and white. Features like 'fixin to' (about to), double modals ('might could'), and the habitual 'be' in African American Vernacular English have roots in West African language structures.","map_center":[33.0,-84.0],"map_zoom":5,"time_point":1800,"highlighted_entities":["eng"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}},{"text":"The slave trade's linguistic legacy is complex and enduring: African-origin words in Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French; vibrant creole languages; African American English; and preserved African languages in religious contexts. From destruction came creation — new languages born from unimaginable suffering.","map_center":[15.0,-45.0],"map_zoom":2,"time_point":2000,"highlighted_entities":["eng","por","spa","fra"],"layer_config":{"layers":["languages"]}}]
